passage:
Subject: Shift pilot proposal for Floor 2

Dear Joseph,

Before we change the roster for the whole floor, I would like to test it with one team first. Here is my plan. Team B, nine people, moves to the new pattern from the first of next month for four weeks. Team A stays as it is. Every week I will count absences and handover errors, meaning forms filled in wrongly or tasks missed at shift change, for both teams, and ask Team B one short question. At the end of the month I will bring you the numbers side by side, and we can decide whether to extend, adjust or drop the change. I would rather learn on nine people than on ninety.

Regards,
Minakshi

qa.q: How many people are in Team B?
What does Minakshi hope to gain by running a pilot?
qa.a: Minakshi wants to learn from a small group first, so that any problems affect fewer people.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if Team B's numbers improve only slightly?
qa.a: Minakshi could extend the pilot or ask Team B which part helped, before deciding about the whole floor.

qa.q: How might a Team B member feel about being in the pilot?
qa.a: A Team B member might feel curious or nervous about the new pattern, but the weekly question gives them a voice.

grounding: Shows a manager planning a month-long pilot with one team, tracking absences and handover errors, before wider use.

subtype: Approach: runs a pilot with a small group before a full rollout [Action]
passage:
Shalini, you asked on your show how I made a big change at the call centre without a riot. Let Rafiq explain.
When I became floor manager, everyone hated the rotating night shifts. I had an idea: fixed shifts, with people choosing morning or evening for three months at a time. But the floor has a hundred and twenty people. If I was wrong, all of them would suffer.
So I asked one team of fifteen to try it for a month. Only them. Everyone else stayed on the old rota.
Every week I tracked two things for both groups: how many people called in absent, and how many handover mistakes happened between shifts. After four weeks, the pilot team had half the absences of the others, but handover mistakes went up at first, because the evening people didn't know the morning people.
So I added a ten-minute overlap at shift change. Then I rolled it out to the whole floor.

qa.q: How many people were in the pilot team?
How was Rafiq feeling about changing shifts for the whole floor at once?
qa.a: Rafiq was worried that if the idea was wrong, all hundred and twenty people would suffer.

qa.q: Why was piloting with one team better than changing the whole floor?
qa.a: It showed both the benefit and a hidden problem, the handover mistakes, on a small group, so the overlap fix was ready before the full rollout.

qa.q: How might the pilot team have experienced the month?
qa.a: They likely enjoyed fixed shifts and felt less worn out, but struggled at first with handovers to people they didn't know.

grounding: It shows a young manager testing a new shift schedule with one team for a month, tracking absences and handover errors, before applying it to the whole floor.

subtype: Approach: runs a pilot with a small group before a full rollout [Action]
passage:
I'm Vijay, and I've worked the packing floor at the warehouse for three years. Last spring our new shift manager, Alka, did something I hadn't seen a manager do before.
She wanted to change our shifts from twelve hours to eight. Half of us liked the idea, half hated it. Instead of changing everyone, she picked only my team, Team C, to try it for four weeks.
She put a sheet on the wall by the time clock. Every day, the supervisors wrote how many people were absent and how many parcels went out wrong at shift change. Same sheet for Team C and for the other teams.
By week four, Team C had fewer absences, but we also had more wrong parcels at the handover, because the change came at a busy hour. Alka moved the change time an hour earlier and then rolled it out to all five teams.
I don't know if she was nervous. She checked that sheet every single morning.

qa.q: How many weeks did Team C try the new shifts?
qa.a: Team C tried it for four weeks.

qa.q: What might Alka checking the sheet every single morning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt careful and perhaps anxious to get it right, though Vijay can't say for sure.

qa.q: Why was moving the change time before the full rollout a good step?
qa.a: The pilot showed handover mistakes at a busy hour, so fixing that first meant all five teams got a better schedule.

qa.q: How might Team C have felt being chosen for the trial?
qa.a: Team C may have felt trusted and a bit tested, getting the new shifts first and seeing their own numbers on the wall.

grounding: It shows a young manager piloting a new shift schedule with one team for a month, tracking absences and handover errors before rolling it out to everyone.
